scenarios.title: All Answers at Once?
scenarios.situation: A startup pitch claims their quantum processor 'tries all answers at once, so it solves every problem instantly.' An investor asks you to sanity-check the claim before a term sheet.
scenarios.prompt: What is the technically honest correction?
evidence: Review the relevant quantum documentation.
choices: Misleading: a superposition holds many computational paths, but measurement reveals only one sample from a probability distribution. Without interference choreography amplifying the right answer, parallelism buys nothing — which is why quantum speedups are rare and problem-specific, not general.
Correct — superposition means every problem is solved in parallel instantly.
Correct for search problems, wrong for everything else.
Wrong — quantum computers are slower than classical ones at everything.
scenarios.why: The Born rule is the whole story: measuring |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|², collapsing the state. You can compute on all possibilities in superposition, but reading the answer out reveals one sample. Every real algorithm — Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, Shor — is an interference pattern designed by hand: amplitudes for wrong answers cancel, the right answer reinforces, and then the measurement pays out.
scenarios.hint: If the machine 'tried everything,' how would you read the answer back out?

scenarios.title: Vector, Not Switch
scenarios.situation: A junior engineer describes a qubit as 'a bit that is 0 and 1 at the same time.' She's about to design a quantum circuit simulator based on that mental model.
scenarios.prompt: What should she understand instead?
evidence: Review the relevant quantum documentation.
choices: A qubit's state is |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1 — a precise geometric statement: the qubit points somewhere on the Bloch sphere. Every single-qubit operation is a rotation of that arrow. The '0 and 1 at once' slogan is not a useful engineering model.
The slogan is fine; simulators don't need the geometry.
A qubit is exactly a probabilistic classical bit.
A qubit is a bit with three values: 0, 1, and both.
scenarios.why: The Bloch sphere is the working model: north pole |0⟩, south pole |1⟩, and every other point a distinct superposition with definite complex amplitudes. Gates are rotations. This precision matters — interference, the real trick of quantum algorithms, is choreography of those amplitudes, and you cannot choreograph what you model as a slogan.
scenarios.hint: What does a Hadamard gate do to the arrow?

scenarios.title: Shor vs. Your Passwords
scenarios.situation: After reading about Shor's algorithm (1994), a client's CISO asks: 'Does this mean all our encryption is already broken? Should we re-encrypt everything with AES-256 today?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the accurate answer?
evidence: Review the relevant quantum documentation.
choices: No — and AES isn't the problem. Shor breaks RSA/ECC in principle, but only on a fault-tolerant machine that does not exist. Symmetric encryption (AES) and hashing are only quadratically weakened by Grover's algorithm. The honest statement: public-key cryptography has a known expiration date — which is why NIST finalized post-quantum standards (FIPS 203/204/205) on August 13, 2024, and the migration of public-key infrastructure is the real work.
Yes — Shor breaks all encryption, so re-encrypt everything immediately.
Yes for RSA, and AES-256 is also fully broken by Grover's algorithm.
No — quantum computers will never threaten any encryption.
scenarios.why: Scope the threat precisely: Shor's polynomial-time factoring and discrete-log algorithm targets public-key systems (RSA, ECC); Grover gives only a quadratic speedup against symmetric crypto, which larger key sizes absorb. The 46-year arc from Feynman's 1980 suggestion to the 2024 NIST standards is the story of a threat seen coming decades out — the migration, not panic, is the response.
scenarios.hint: Which of the client's systems use public-key crypto, and which use symmetric?

scenarios.title: The Qubit Count Press Release
scenarios.situation: A hardware vendor announces a 2,000-qubit processor and claims to be '2,000 times closer to breaking RSA than last year's 1,000-qubit machine.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you grade the claim?
evidence: Review the relevant quantum documentation.
choices: Misleading. A thousand noisy physical qubits are not one-thousandth of the way to a cryptographically relevant machine — without error correction, qubit count alone says almost nothing about capability. Logical (error-corrected) qubits are the metric that matters, and the industry still counts those in single digits.
Accurate — qubit count is the standard progress metric.
Accurate, but only for superconducting qubits, not trapped ions.
Wrong direction — more qubits make RSA harder to break.
scenarios.why: Decoherence is why the machines are hard: a qubit stays quantum only while isolated, and heat, stray fields, even control wiring collapse superpositions toward classical noise. Error correction protects quantum information without ever reading it (no-cloning forbids copying it out to check). Until logical qubits scale, physical qubit counts are a press-release metric, not a capability metric.
scenarios.hint: How many of those 2,000 qubits are logical — error-corrected — qubits?

scenarios.title: Judging a 'Quantum Advantage' Claim
scenarios.situation: A lab press release claims 'quantum advantage' on an optimization problem: their 80-qubit device beat the best classical result — but the classical baseline is from 2019, the problem instance was chosen by the hardware team, and no independent group has reproduced it.
scenarios.prompt: You are asked to grade the claim, capstone-style.
evidence: Review the relevant quantum documentation.
choices: Contested at best. The checklist: is the classical baseline current (remember how improved classical simulations narrowed Google's 2019 Sycamore 'supremacy' claim on random-circuit sampling — a benchmark with no practical use)? Was the problem chosen neutrally? Is it reproduced independently? Does the task have practical use? Supremacy on a useless or cherry-picked task is a physics milestone, not a product — and certainly not a verdict.
Accept it — 80 qubits beating classical is advantage by definition.
Reject it — quantum advantage is impossible in principle.
Accept it, but only if the lab publishes the circuit depth.
scenarios.why: This is the capstone skill: grade hype with a fixed rubric. Google's 2019 Sycamore result demonstrated a task hard for classical supercomputers at the time — and subsequent classical improvements narrowed the gap. The pattern repeats: baseline freshness, problem selection, independent reproduction, and practical utility are the four questions, asked in that order, every time.
scenarios.hint: What would change your grade — in either direction?

scenarios.title: You Cannot Copy the Qubit
scenarios.situation: An engineer proposes debugging a quantum program the classical way: copy the qubit register mid-computation, inspect the copy, and continue. Another proposes backing up quantum state to disk 'just in case.'
scenarios.prompt: Why do both proposals fail?
evidence: Review the relevant quantum documentation.
choices: The no-cloning theorem (proved 1982): no operation copies an unknown quantum state |ψ⟩ into |ψ⟩|ψ⟩. It's a theorem, not a hardware limitation — no variables can be copied, no state inspected mid-computation, and error correction must protect quantum information without ever reading it. It is also the bedrock of quantum cryptography: eavesdropping disturbs the state and reveals itself.
They fail only on current hardware; future machines will allow copying.
Copying works but is too slow to be useful for debugging.
The proposals are fine — the theorem only applies to entangled states.
scenarios.why: No-cloning is what makes quantum computing feel alien and what makes quantum key distribution possible: any attempt to read an unknown state disturbs it. Debugging therefore means reasoning about circuits and statistics of measurement outcomes — never peeking at the state itself. Design your tools around the theorem, not against it.
scenarios.hint: If you can't copy the state, what *can* you log?

lessons.title: Quantum Computing: Qubits, Algorithms & the Cryptographic Future — Core concepts
concepts: The qubit is a vector, not a switch: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1 — a point on the Bloch sphere, and every single-qubit gate a rotation of that arrow.

The Born rule: measurement returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|², collapsing the state. A million measurements reveal the probabilities, never the amplitudes — which is why 'trying all answers at once' buys nothing by itself.
n qubits hold one vector in a 2ⁿ-dimensional space. That exponential dimension is the entire reason quantum computing is interesting — and the entire reason it is hard to simulate classically.

Interference is the real trick: quantum algorithms arrange amplitudes so wrong answers cancel and the right answer reinforces. Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, and Shor are interference patterns designed by hand.
No-cloning (theorem, 1982): an unknown quantum state cannot be copied. No mid-computation inspection, no backups — and the bedrock of quantum cryptography.

Decoherence: qubits stay quantum only while isolated. The hardware war is fought against heat, stray fields, and control wiring — which is why logical (error-corrected) qubits, still counted in single digits, are the metric that matters.

The 46-year arc: 1980 (Benioff/Feynman) → 1985 (Deutsch) → 1994 (Shor) → 1996 (Grover) → 2019 (Sycamore) → 2022 (Nobel for entanglement experiments) → August 13, 2024 (NIST finalizes FIPS 203/204/205 post-quantum standards) → 2026: no fault-tolerant machine exists.

example.code:
pip install qiskit qiskit-aer
python3 - <<'EOF'
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)          # superposition on qubit 0
qc.cx(0, 1)      # entangle: Bell pair
qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
counts = AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=1000).result().get_counts()
print(counts)    # ~{'00': 500, '11': 500}: correlated, never 01/10
EOF
example.walkthrough: Build a Bell pair: Hadamard puts qubit 0 in superposition, CNOT entangles it with qubit 1. The measurement statistics show perfect correlation — 00 or 11, never mixed — the signature of entanglement that no classical description reproduces. This is the open-source lab (Qiskit) the track's Module 9 walks through.

pitfalls: Common trap: 'superposition = trying everything at once.' Measurement yields one sample; only interference choreography extracts an answer.
Common trap: 'more physical qubits = closer to breaking RSA.' Without error correction, qubit count says almost nothing; count logical qubits.
Common trap: 'Shor means all encryption is broken.' It targets public-key crypto on a machine that doesn't exist; symmetric crypto is only quadratically weakened.
Common trap: 'quantum computers will replace classical ones.' They accelerate specific structured problems and remain coprocessors for the foreseeable future.

lessons.title: Qubits: Beyond Bits
concepts: A qubit is the quantum unit of information — unlike a classical bit (0 OR 1), a qubit exists in superposition (0 AND 1 simultaneously) until measured
Superposition is described by probability amplitudes (α|0⟩ + β|1⟩) where |α|² + |β|² = 1 — measurement collapses the state to 0 or 1 with those probabilities
The Bloch sphere visualizes a single qubit state as a point on a sphere — the north pole is |0⟩, south pole is |1⟩, equator is equal superposition
Multiple qubits create exponentially large state spaces: n qubits represent 2ⁿ amplitudes simultaneously — this is the source of quantum parallelism

example.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.h(0)  # Hadamard: |0> -> (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2)
qc.measure(0, 0)
print(qc)
example.walkthrough: The Hadamard gate creates superposition from |0⟩. Run this circuit 1000 times and you'll get roughly 500 zeros and 500 ones — true quantum randomness, not pseudorandom.

Confusing quantum randomness with classical pseudorandomness — quantum measurement is fundamentally non-deterministic

lessons.title: Entanglement: Spooky Correlation
concepts: Entanglement links qubits so measuring one instantly determines the other's state, regardless of distance — Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance'
The Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 is the simplest entangled pair: measure the first qubit, and the second is guaranteed to match
Entanglement is a resource, not communication — you cannot use it to send information faster than light (no-communication theorem)
Entangled qubits enable quantum teleportation, superdense coding, and the exponential speedup in many quantum algorithms

example.code:
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)       # Superposition on qubit 0
qc.cx(0, 1)   # CNOT: entangle qubit 1 with qubit 0
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])
example.walkthrough: The H + CNOT sequence creates a Bell pair. Measure both qubits 1000 times: you'll see only 00 and 11 (never 01 or 10) — perfect correlation.

pitfalls: Thinking entanglement allows instant messaging — measurement outcomes are correlated but random, carrying no controllable signal
Confusing entanglement with classical correlation — entangled particles violate Bell inequalities, proving non-locality
Assuming entanglement is fragile and useless — error correction codes protect entangled states for computation
lessons.try_it: Create a Bell pair in Qiskit and verify the correlation. Then add noise and observe how decoherence breaks entanglement.

lessons.title: Quantum Gates: The Building Blocks
concepts: Quantum gates are unitary operations (reversible) applied to qubits — unlike classical gates (AND, OR) which lose information
Single-qubit gates rotate the Bloch sphere: X (bit flip), Z (phase flip), H (superposition), T (π/8 phase)
Two-qubit gates create entanglement: CNOT (controlled-NOT) flips the target if control is |1⟩; CZ applies phase conditionally
Universal gate sets (e.g., {H, T, CNOT}) can approximate any quantum operation — this is the quantum equivalent of NAND universality

example.code:
# Bell state circuit with explicit gates
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)      # |00> -> (|00> + |10>)/sqrt(2)
qc.cx(0, 1)  # -> (|00> + |11>)/sqrt(2)
# Statevector: [0.707, 0, 0, 0.707]
example.walkthrough: Trace the statevector through each gate. After H: amplitudes are [0.707, 0, 0.707, 0]. After CNOT: [0.707, 0, 0, 0.707] — the |10⟩ amplitude moved to |11⟩.

pitfalls: Treating quantum gates like classical gates — quantum gates must be reversible (unitary); you can't have a quantum AND gate
Forgetting that gate order matters — quantum operations don't commute; H then X differs from X then H
Ignoring the global phase — mathematically irrelevant but matters for controlled operations

lessons.title: Quantum Algorithms: Shor's Algorithm
concepts: Shor's algorithm factors large integers exponentially faster than classical methods — threatening RSA encryption
The algorithm reduces factoring to period-finding: find the period r of f(x) = aˣ mod N, then compute gcd(a^(r/2) ± 1, N)
Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) finds the period efficiently — this is the quantum speedup core
A sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer could break 2048-bit RSA in hours vs. billions of years classically

example.code:
Shor's algorithm for N=15, a=7:
  1. Find period of 7^x mod 15: sequence 1,7,4,13,1,... period r=4
  2. Compute gcd(7^(4/2)+1, 15) = gcd(50,15) = 5
  3. Compute gcd(7^(4/2)-1, 15) = gcd(48,15) = 3
  4. Factors: 15 = 3 × 5
example.walkthrough: The quantum part is step 1 (period-finding via QFT). Steps 2-4 are classical post-processing. For N=15, a quantum computer finds r=4 using superposition to evaluate f(x) for all x simultaneously.

pitfalls: Thinking Shor's breaks all encryption — it threatens RSA/ECC (factoring/discrete log), but symmetric crypto (AES) is only weakened (Grover's gives quadratic speedup)
Assuming quantum computers can already break RSA — we need millions of physical qubits for fault tolerance; current machines have ~1000 noisy qubits
Confusing Shor's with Grover's — Shor's is exponential speedup for factoring; Grover's is quadratic for unstructured search

lessons.title: Quantum Algorithms: Grover's Search
concepts: Grover's algorithm searches an unsorted database of N items in O(√N) time vs. O(N) classically — a quadratic speedup
The algorithm uses amplitude amplification: iteratively boost the probability of the target state while suppressing others
Applications include: brute-force key search, SAT solving, and as a subroutine in other quantum algorithms
For AES-128, Grover's reduces effective security to 64 bits — AES-256 remains quantum-safe (128-bit effective)

example.code:
# Grover's for 2 qubits, target |11>
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h([0,1])           # Uniform superposition
# Oracle: mark |11>
qc.cz(0,1)            # Phase flip for |11>
# Diffusion: amplify
qc.h([0,1]); qc.x([0,1]); qc.cz(0,1); qc.x([0,1]); qc.h([0,1])
example.walkthrough: After one Grover iteration on 2 qubits, the |11⟩ amplitude goes from 0.5 to ~1.0. For larger N, repeat ~π√N/4 times for optimal amplification.

pitfalls: Expecting exponential speedup — Grover's is quadratic, not exponential; it doesn't make NP-hard problems easy
Over-rotating — too many iterations DECREASES success probability; the optimal count is precise
Thinking Grover's needs a structured database — it works on unstructured search where the oracle can recognize the target

lessons.title: Superposition in Depth
concepts: Superposition is not 'being in two states' — it's a single quantum state described by a linear combination of basis states
The coefficients (amplitudes) are complex numbers; measurement probabilities are their squared magnitudes
Relative phase between amplitudes matters — it determines interference patterns in algorithms
Decoherence destroys superposition by entangling the qubit with the environment — this is why quantum computers need isolation

example.code:
qc = QuantumCircuit(1)
qc.h(0)   # (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2), phase = 0
qc2 = QuantumCircuit(1)
qc2.h(0); qc2.z(0)  # (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2), phase = π
example.walkthrough: Both circuits measure 50/50, but the states differ by phase. Apply another H: first returns to |0⟩, second goes to |1⟩ — phase drives interference.

pitfalls: Ignoring phase — phase is invisible in single measurement but critical for multi-qubit interference
Thinking superposition is fragile and useless — algorithms are designed to exploit superposition before decoherence
Confusing mixed states with superposition — mixed states are classical uncertainty; superposition is quantum coherence

lessons.title: Quantum Fourier Transform
concepts: QFT is the quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform — it reveals periodicities in quantum states
QFT on n qubits uses O(n²) gates vs. O(n2ⁿ) classically — exponential speedup for the transform itself
QFT is the engine inside Shor's algorithm (period-finding) and quantum phase estimation
The inverse QFT is used to read out results — it's as important as the forward transform

example.code:
from qiskit.circuit.library import QFT
qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.append(QFT(3), [0,1,2])
print(qc.decompose())
example.walkthrough: The QFT circuit uses Hadamard gates and controlled phase rotations. For 3 qubits, it creates intricate interference patterns that encode frequency information.

pitfalls: Thinking QFT outputs classical data — it transforms quantum states; you need inverse QFT + measurement to extract results
Confusing QFT with classical FFT applications — QFT is for quantum period-finding, not signal processing
Ignoring the precision requirements — QFT needs high-fidelity gates; noise destroys the interference pattern

lessons.title: Superconducting Qubits
concepts: Superconducting qubits use Josephson junctions cooled to ~10mK — colder than deep space
Transmon qubits are the most common type, used by IBM and Google
Coherence times are ~100 microseconds — enough for ~1000 gate operations
Error rates are ~0.1% per gate — too high for large algorithms without error correction

pitfalls: Focusing only on qubit count — error rates and connectivity matter more for useful computation
Thinking dilution refrigerators are optional — superconducting qubits MUST be near absolute zero
Assuming hardware improvements are linear — error correction thresholds require exponential precision gains

Hybrid approaches combine classical + post-quantum for defense in depth during transition

lessons.title: Qiskit Fundamentals
concepts: Qiskit is IBM's open-source quantum SDK — the most widely used quantum programming framework
Core workflow: build circuit → transpile for backend → execute → analyze results
Aer simulator lets you test without hardware; real backends available via IBM Quantum
Qiskit patterns: initialization, unitary evolution, measurement — every algorithm follows this structure

example.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])

sim = AerSimulator()
tqc = transpile(qc, sim)
result = sim.run(tqc, shots=1000).result()
print(result.get_counts())
example.walkthrough: This is the complete workflow: circuit definition, transpilation (optimize for backend), execution (1000 shots), result analysis (counts dictionary).

pitfalls: Skipping transpilation — circuits must be optimized for specific backend topology and gate sets
Running too few shots — quantum results are statistical; 100 shots gives noisy estimates
Not checking backend properties — qubit connectivity affects which CNOTs are possible

lessons.title: Surface Codes
concepts: Surface codes are the leading approach to fault-tolerant quantum computation — they encode one logical qubit in a 2D grid of physical qubits
The code distance d determines error protection: a distance-d surface code corrects ⌊(d-1)/2⌋ errors
Syndrome measurements detect errors without collapsing the logical state — ancilla qubits extract error information
Threshold theorem: if physical error rates are below ~1%, arbitrarily long computations are possible with sufficient overhead

example.walkthrough: We're in the NISQ era (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) — useful computation without full error correction, but limited scale.

pitfalls: Thinking more physical qubits automatically helps — without error correction, more qubits means more noise
Ignoring the overhead — fault tolerance requires 1000x physical qubits per logical qubit
Assuming NISQ devices can run Shor's — they can't; we need fault tolerance first

lessons.title: Quantum Machine Learning
concepts: QML explores whether quantum computers can accelerate ML tasks — results are mixed and problem-dependent
Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and QAOA are hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for optimization
Quantum kernel methods map data to high-dimensional Hilbert spaces for classification
Barren plateaus are a major challenge — gradients vanish exponentially with qubit count in many QML models

pitfalls: Assuming QML always beats classical ML — advantage is problem-specific and unproven for most tasks
Ignoring barren plateaus — many variational circuits can't be trained at scale
Confusing quantum-inspired with quantum — tensor networks run on classical hardware

lessons.title: Quantum Networking
concepts: Quantum networks distribute entanglement between distant nodes — the foundation for a quantum internet
Quantum repeaters overcome photon loss in fiber — they use entanglement swapping to extend range
QKD (Quantum Key Distribution) provides information-theoretic secure key exchange — eavesdropping is detectable
The quantum internet would enable distributed quantum computing and ultra-precise sensing networks

example.walkthrough: QKD doesn't encrypt data — it distributes keys with provable security. The keys then encrypt via one-time pad or AES.

pitfalls: Thinking QKD encrypts messages — it distributes keys; encryption is separate
Ignoring distance limits — fiber QKD is limited to ~100km without repeaters
Assuming QKD is unhackable — implementation flaws (side channels) have been exploited

lessons.title: Simulating Molecules
concepts: Quantum simulation was Feynman's original motivation — classical computers can't efficiently simulate quantum systems
VQE finds molecular ground states by variationally optimizing a parameterized quantum circuit
Applications: drug discovery, catalyst design, material science — wherever electron behavior matters
Current limit: small molecules (H2, LiH); useful chemistry needs 100+ logical qubits

Ignoring the measurement overhead — VQE requires many circuit repetitions

lessons.title: Defining Advantage
concepts: Quantum supremacy: solving a problem faster on quantum hardware than any classical supercomputer (Google, 2019, 53 qubits)
Quantum advantage: solving a USEFUL problem faster — a higher bar than supremacy
The advantage is problem-specific — quantum computers aren't universally faster
Classical algorithms improve too — 'supremacy' claims have been challenged by better classical methods

pitfalls: Thinking supremacy means quantum computers are 'better' — it's a narrow technical milestone
Ignoring classical improvements — each supremacy claim spurs better classical algorithms
Assuming advantage is inevitable for all problems — most problems get no quantum speedup

labs.objective: Install Qiskit, build a Bell-pair circuit, simulate 1000 shots, and interpret the correlated statistics.
steps: Install qiskit and qiskit-aer in a fresh virtual environment.

Add a one-paragraph note to the file explaining, in your own words, why this correlation has no classical explanation.

cheatsheet: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, |α|² + |β|² = 1. Qubit = point on Bloch sphere; gates = rotations.
Born rule: measurement pays out probabilities |α|²/|β|² and collapses the state.
n qubits = one vector in 2ⁿ dimensions. Entanglement = joint states that don't factor.
Interference is the trick: wrong answers cancel, right answer reinforces.
No-cloning (1982): unknown states can't be copied — no peeking, bedrock of quantum crypto.
Decoherence: isolation is everything. Count logical qubits, not physical ones.
Shor → public-key expiry (fault-tolerant machine needed). Grover → quadratic hit on symmetric only.
1980 suggestion → 2024 NIST FIPS 203/204/205 standards. 2026: no fault-tolerant machine exists.

glossary.def: The quantum unit of information: a normalized vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, visualized on the Bloch sphere.
A qubit state combining basis states with complex amplitudes; measurement collapses it per the Born rule.
Joint multi-qubit states that cannot be described as independent single-qubit states.
Amplitude cancellation/reinforcement arranged by quantum algorithms to amplify correct answers.
Loss of quantum behavior through interaction with the environment.
An error-corrected qubit built from many physical qubits; the capability metric that matters.
Classical algorithms believed resistant to quantum attack; NIST standardized ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA in 2024.

checklist: I can write the qubit state equation and explain the Bloch sphere.
I can state the Born rule and why 'try all answers at once' is misleading.
I can explain interference as the mechanism behind Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, and Shor.
I scope Shor's threat correctly: public-key, fault-tolerant machine, not yet real.
I grade advantage claims with the four-question rubric.

simulations.title: The Bell pair that wasn't entangled
simulations.brief: Your Bell-state circuit should produce perfectly correlated measurements. Instead the two qubits read 00, 01, 10, 11 with equal probability — no correlation at all.

steps.symptom: Measurement outcomes uniform over 00/01/10/11 — zero correlation.
evidence: Circuit diagram
q0: X gate, then CNOT with q0 as control and q1 as target. No Hadamard anywhere
State tomography
The two-qubit state factors as a product state — no entanglement present
Single-qubit check
q0 measures 1 with probability ~1.0, q1 measures 0 — the X gate fired, the CNOT did nothing observable
options: Add a Hadamard gate on q0 before the CNOT to create the superposition the entanglement needs
Add a second CNOT — more entanglement gates means more entanglement
Increase the shot count — the correlation is there, just undersampled
Measure in the X basis instead of Z — the correlation hides in the wrong basis
steps.explain: CNOT entangles only when the control is in superposition. With q0 in the |1> state, CNOT is just a classical flip — the output is the product state |10>, which measures with zero correlation. The Hadamard puts q0 into superposition first; then the CNOT creates the Bell state.

simulations.debrief: Entanglement needs superposition first. A CNOT on computational-basis inputs is classical logic; the Hadamard before it is what makes the magic. When correlations vanish, check the gates before the entangler.

simulations.title: Shor's algorithm gives wrong factors
simulations.brief: Your Shor's implementation factors 15 correctly on the simulator but returns garbage on the real 5-qubit device.

steps.symptom: Correct factors on the noiseless simulator; wrong answers on hardware.
evidence: Shot count
100 shots on hardware
Device calibration
Two-qubit gate error 1.8%, readout error 3.2%, T1 ~80us
Circuit depth
Depth 94 after transpilation — near the coherence limit
options: Increase shots to 1024+, add readout error mitigation, and reduce depth with a better transpiler pass
Run the same 100 shots five times and take a majority vote
Switch to a different 5-qubit device and hope for better calibration
Factor a smaller number — 15 is too ambitious for this hardware
steps.explain: 100 shots on noisy hardware cannot resolve the period-finding peaks, and depth 94 at 1.8% gate error means most runs are corrupted before measurement. More shots resolve the distribution, readout mitigation cleans the counts, and shallower circuits survive decoherence.

simulations.debrief: Hardware runs are statistics plus noise management: enough shots to resolve the answer, error mitigation for the readout, and circuits shallow enough to outrun decoherence. The simulator is the theory; the device is the experiment.

simulations.title: Pick the quantum algorithm
simulations.brief: You need to find one marked item in an unstructured database of one million entries. Choose the quantum approach.

choices.label: Grover's algorithm — quadratic speedup, ~1,000 oracle queries
choices.feedback: Correct: Grover's gives the proven quadratic speedup for unstructured search — square root of N queries instead of N.

choices.label: Shor's algorithm — it factors fast, so it searches fast
choices.feedback: Shor's factors integers; it does not search unstructured data. Algorithm choice follows the problem structure, not the hype.

simulations.debrief: Match the algorithm to the problem: Grover for unstructured search, Shor for factoring, QAOA/VQE for optimization and chemistry. Quantum advantage is problem-specific, not universal.

simulations.title: Run a quantum job
simulations.brief: Put the quantum job workflow in the order that produces a trustworthy hardware result.

items: Transpile the circuit for the target backend
Analyze the mitigated counts for the answer
Choose the shot count from the precision needed
Apply readout error mitigation to the counts
Execute the job on the backend

simulations.debrief: Transpile for the hardware first (depth and connectivity decide feasibility), size the shots for the precision you need, execute, mitigate the readout errors, then analyze. Analyzing raw noisy counts is reading tea leaves.

simulations.title: Review the circuit config
simulations.brief: This circuit config is headed to a noisy 5-qubit backend. Click the misconfigured lines (2 issues to find).

steps.config:
qubits: 5
depth: 200
shots: 1024
error_mitigation: none
transpiler: basic
backend: noisy_simulator

issues.description: Depth 200 on a noisy backend — decoherence destroys the state long before measurement.
issues.fix: Reduce depth (better transpilation, shallower ansatz) to fit the coherence budget.

issues.description: No error mitigation on a noisy backend — readout and gate errors corrupt the counts unchecked.
issues.fix: Enable readout error mitigation at minimum.

simulations.debrief: Noisy hardware has a coherence budget: deep circuits plus no mitigation equals noise. Keep circuits shallow and mitigate what the hardware cannot avoid.
